title: Making Handoffs Honest About What Is Unknown
summary: Why "should be fine" in a handoff hides a guess, and how to label each claim as verified, assumed or unknown so the next owner knows what to trust and what to test.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The handoff looked clean. Branch, ticket, test command, next owner, all there. On day two the next owner hit the real question: had anyone confirmed how the payment provider handles partial refunds? The old note said "refund flow handled." It turned out someone had tested the full-refund case and assumed partial refunds would behave the same way. The note was tidy. It just sounded more certain than the work behind it.

Unknowns are a normal part of real work. The trouble starts when they hide behind confident wording, or sit in a chat thread the next person will never scroll back to. Then the receiver inherits a guess without knowing it's a guess. This post is about writing down what you don't know as carefully as what you do. For the general shape of a good handoff (status, decisions, next step), see the sibling post Making Handoffs Easier to Receive.

Vague words hide very different odds

In 1951, the CIA's Board of National Estimates wrote that a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia that year "should be considered a serious possibility." A few days later, a State Department official asked Sherman Kent, one of the authors, what odds they had in mind. Kent's own answer was about 65 to 35 in favor of an attack, and the official was jolted, because his team had read the phrase as much lower odds. When Kent asked his colleagues on the Board, who had all agreed to the wording, their answers ranged from about 20 to 80 all the way to 80 to 20 (Words of Estimative Probability, 1964).

Kent's fix was a small table that tied words to numbers: "almost certain" meant about 93%, "probable" about 75%, "chances about even" about 50%, "probably not" about 30%. You don't need a CIA chart for a ticket handoff, but the lesson travels well. "Should be fine," "mostly done" and "handled" mean different things to different people. If you know your confidence, say it in a way nobody can misread.

Sort every claim into three buckets

A simple structure covers most handoffs. Put each important claim in one of three groups:

  • Verified: you checked it, and you can say how. "Full refunds work on staging, tested with the provider's sandbox card."
  • Assumed: reasonable, not proven. "Partial refunds probably use the same endpoint. Haven't tested it."
  • Unknown: nobody knows yet. "How refunds behave after the provider's 30-day window. Waiting on their support team, ticket linked."

The labels do real work. The receiver can build on the verified items without retesting them, test the assumptions first, and chase or plan around the unknowns. Without labels, they either retest everything to be safe or trust everything and get burned.

A note that's honest about its gaps

Changed: refund API wired up, behind the refunds_v2 flag.
Verified: full refund on staging with sandbox card.
Assumed: partial refunds use the same endpoint (not tested).
Unknown: behavior after 30 days. Asked provider support Tuesday, no answer yet.
Next: test a partial refund on staging before anything else.
Owner: you from Monday. I'm reachable in the thread until Friday.

Run a two-minute premortem on your own note

Psychologist Gary Klein describes the premortem in Harvard Business Review: before a project starts, the team pretends it has already failed and writes down every reason why. Assuming the failure already happened makes it easier to name problems people would otherwise keep to themselves.

The same trick works on a handoff in two minutes. Read your note as the receiver and imagine it's next Thursday and they're stuck. What tripped them up? An untested edge case, an approval you thought was coming, a config value that only exists on your machine? Whatever comes to mind goes into the Assumed or Unknown bucket.

Written-down assumptions make for better postmortems

Honest handoffs also lower the temperature when something goes wrong. If an assumption turns out wrong and it was written down, the team can look at why it seemed reasonable and whether it should have been checked sooner. That's a conversation about the process. When the assumption only surfaces after the failure, the conversation tends to turn into "who said this was done?", and nobody learns much from that.

The template matters less than the habit. Changed, verified, assumed, unknown, next action, owner fits in one message. What counts is refusing to make uncertainty invisible because the note looks neater without it.

Before you send your next handoff

  • Search your note for "should," "mostly" and "handled," and replace each with a verified, assumed or unknown label.
  • For every verified item, add how you checked it.
  • For every unknown, add who you asked and when.
  • Imagine the receiver stuck next Thursday and write down what stopped them.

faqs.q: Why include unknowns in a handoff?
faqs.a: Because the receiver inherits them either way. If an unknown is written down, they can test it, chase it or plan around it. If it hides behind confident wording like "handled," they inherit a guess without knowing it's a guess and usually find out later, when it costs more.

faqs.q: How should I label uncertainty in a handoff note?
faqs.a: Sort each important claim into verified (you checked it and can say how), assumed (reasonable but not proven) or unknown (nobody knows yet, with who was asked and when). The receiver can then build on verified items, test assumptions first and follow up on unknowns.

Often not. Sherman Kent's 1964 CIA essay describes colleagues who all agreed on the phrase "serious possibility" yet meant odds ranging from about 20 to 80 up to 80 to 20. Plain labels or explicit numbers are harder to misread than words like "should be fine" or "mostly done."

faqs.q: What is a quick premortem for a handoff?
faqs.a: Gary Klein's premortem asks a team to assume a project has already failed and list why. For a handoff, read your note as the receiver, imagine they are stuck a week from now, and write down what stopped them. Anything you think of goes into the assumed or unknown section.
